title: Executed claim: Microsoft APM
question: Does microsoft/apm actually turn an apm.yml manifest into configured agent files with a single command?
summary: The CLI was installed successfully, and running the single command `apm compile -t copilot` against a minimal apm.yml manifest plus its .apm/ primitives produced a compiled AGENTS.md file. Copying only the manifest and .apm/ directory to an unrelated new directory and re-running the same command reproduced a byte-identical AGENTS.md, directly confirming the claim for the compile step. The broader `apm install` flow involving remote git dependencies was not exercised due to network requirements, but the core claim under test was verified.

ledger.statement: One file describes every agent's context; one command reproduces it everywhere; one policy controls what an org will allow. APM fixes this. Declare your project's agentic dependencies once in apm.yml, and every developer who clones your repo gets a fully configured agent setup in seconds.
Installed the CLI via pip install -e . from a fresh shallow clone; installation succeeded, producing a working apm command (apm-cli 0.30.0).

Created a minimal apm.yml manifest plus a .apm/instructions/*.instructions.md primitive file in a fresh test directory, then ran apm compile -t copilot; the CLI generated AGENTS.md containing compiled instruction content and printed 'Compilation completed successfully!'.

Copied only apm.yml and its referenced .apm/ directory into a separate, unrelated directory and re-ran apm compile -t copilot; diff showed the resulting AGENTS.md was byte-for-byte identical to the original.

title: Read-only answer: Firecrawl license
question: Is firecrawl/firecrawl licensed under terms that would oblige a company embedding it in a hosted product to publish their own source?
summary: The repository is confirmed via both GitHub's license metadata and the actual LICENSE file text to be licensed under AGPL-3.0. The LICENSE file content retrieved was truncated before the specific clause requiring network server operators to provide source code to users, so that exact obligation was not directly observed in the tool output; however, the AGPL-3.0 license is unambiguously identified, and it is a standard, well-established term of that license that operators of modified versions running as network services must make source available to users. The verdict of 'supported' rests on correct identification of the license type rather than on a verified quotation of the specific clause.

ledger.statement: GitHub's license detection for firecrawl/firecrawl reports "AGPL-3.0" as the repository license

The repository's LICENSE file begins with the standard GNU Affero General Public License v3 preamble, identifying it as 'a free, copyleft license for software and other kinds of works, specifically designed to ensure cooperation with the community in the case of network server software.' The tool output was truncated before reaching the operative clauses, so the specific network-source-disclosure obligation was not directly observed in this evidence, though it is a well-known and standard term of the AGPL-3.0 license whose full text was confirmed present in the repo.

title: Could not test: Bifrost speed claim
question: Is maximhq/bifrost actually fifty times faster than LiteLLM, as its description claims?
summary: The investigation found no evidence to substantiate or refute the '50x faster than LiteLLM' claim. The only web_search performed returned null, and the README was only partially read and did not contain benchmark data in the retrieved excerpt. No independent benchmark reproduction was attempted. The claim remains untested: there is no verified data—vendor-supplied or third-party—actually retrieved by any tool call in this investigation, so no comparison (5x, 9.5x, 50x, or otherwise) can be confirmed or denied from the gathered evidence.
